passages.original: Inscripsere namque - *x alii de rebus, alii de generibus rerum, quos eadem similisque culpa confudit. Namque (ut docuimus) non de rerum generibus,neque de rebus, sed de ser. monibus rerum genera significantibus in hoc opere tractatus habetur, hoc vero Aristoteles ipse declarat cum dicit: Eorum quae secundum nullam complexionem dicuntur, singulum aut substantiam significat,aut quantitatem.Quod si de rebus divisionem faceret,non dixisset significat; res enim significatur, non ipsa significat.IIlud quoque maximo argumento est Aristotelem non de rebus, sed de sermonibus res significantibus speculari,quod ait: Singulum igitur eorum que dicta sunt,ipsum quidem secundum se in nulla affirmatione dicitur,horum antem ad seinvicem complexione affirmatio fit.Resenim sijungantur,affirmationem nullo modo perficiunt,affirmatio namque in oratione est.Quocirca si prædicamenta juncta faciunt affirmationem (affirmatiovero non nisi in oratione est,quae autem junguntur ut affirmatio fiat,hae suntrerumsignificantesvoces)praedicamentorumtractatus non de rebus,sed de vocibus est;male igitur vel de rebus vel rerum generibus inscripserunt.Annotant alii bunc librum legendum ante Topica,quod nimis absurdum est.
passages.english: For some have given it the title "On Things", others "On the Genera of Things", and the same or a similar fault has confused them both. For (as we have shown) this work treats neither of the genera of things nor of things, but of the words that signify the genera of things. Aristotle himself makes this clear when he says: "Of those things which are said without any combination, each signifies either substance or quantity." But if he were making a division of things, he would not have said "signifies"; for a thing is signified, it does not itself signify. This too is a very strong argument that Aristotle is examining not things but the words that signify things, that he says: "Each of the things that have been mentioned is not, by itself, said in any affirmation, but an affirmation comes about from the combination of these with one another." For things, if they are joined, in no way complete an affirmation, since an affirmation is in speech. Therefore, if the predicaments when joined make an affirmation (and an affirmation exists only in speech, and what are joined so that an affirmation may come about are the spoken words that signify things), the treatment of the predicaments is not about things but about spoken words; so they were wrong to give it the title either "On Things" or "On the Genera of Things". Others note that this book should be read before the Topics, which is quite absurd.
passages.notes: The dash and "*x" after "Inscripsere namque" appear to be stray marks or a lacuna in the scan; omitted. "quantitatem" in the quotation stands for the opening of the list of categories (substance, quantity, etc.).

passages.original: Solum autem duobus modis dicitur: semel cum aliquid unum esse dicirnus, ut si dicamus solusest mundus, id est unus ; alio vero modo cum dicimus ad quamdam ab altero divisionem,ut si quis dicat solam me habere tunicam,id eSI,non etiam togam,ad divisionem videlicet togae. Hic ergo Aristoteles posuit dil'ens,Solum nomen commune est,quasi hoc voluisset intelligi non etiam diffinitio, aequivoca enim jungunturnomine,sed diffinitione dissentiunt.Communequoquemultisdiciturmodis.Diciturcommune quod in partes dividitur,et non jam totumcommune est, sed partes ejus propriae singularum,ut domus.
passages.english: Now "only" is said in two ways: once when we say that something is one, as if we say "the world is alone", that is, one; and in another way when we speak with reference to a certain division from something else, as if someone says that he has only a tunic, that is, not a toga as well, namely by distinction from the toga. Here, then, Aristotle put [it] saying, "only the name is common", as if he wished this to be understood: not the definition as well; for equivocals are joined by the name but differ in definition. "Common" too is said in many ways. That is called common which is divided into parts, and then it is no longer common as a whole, but its parts belong individually to each person, as a house.
passages.notes: "dil'ens" read as "dicens".

passages.original: Universale autem est quod aptum est de pluribus praedicari.Particulare vero quod de nullo subjecto prædicatur. Ergo es una complexio universalitatis et subsfantiae, ut sit substantia universalis. Si vero particularis substantiæ copulatur,fit substantia particularis,ut est Socrates vel Plato,et quidquid in substantia individuum reperitur.Atcum miscetur universalitasaccidenti,fit accidens universale,ut scientia,quæ cum sit accidens, et praeteranimam cui accidit esse non possit, tamen universalis est,quod;desubjecta grammaticavelaliis speciebus praedicari poteat.Cum vero particularitas accidenti conjungitur, fit accidens particulare, ut Platonis vel Aristotelis scientia. Fiunt enim quatuor com plexiones,substantia universalis,substantia particularis,accidens universale, accidens particulare, Ut autem accidens iu substantiae naturam transeat, vel substantia in accidens,fieri nullo modo potest,et accidens quidem venit in substantiam, sed non ut substantia fiat: neque enim quoniam color,quod est accidens venitin substantiam,idcirco color jam substantia est.
passages.english: Now the universal is what is apt to be predicated of many things; the particular, what is predicated of no subject. So one combination is of universality and substance, so that there is universal substance. But if [particularity] is joined to substance, particular substance results, such as Socrates or Plato, and whatever individual is found in substance. And when universality is mixed with accident, universal accident results, such as knowledge, which, though it is an accident and cannot exist apart from the soul to which it belongs as an accident, is nevertheless universal, because it can be predicated of grammar, which is subordinate to it, or of other species. But when particularity is joined to accident, particular accident results, such as the knowledge of Plato or of Aristotle. So four combinations arise: universal substance, particular substance, universal accident, particular accident. But that an accident should pass into the nature of substance, or substance into accident, can in no way happen. An accident does indeed come into a substance, but not so as to become substance: for it is not the case that, because colour, which is an accident, comes into a substance, colour is therefore now substance.
passages.notes: 'Si vero particularis substantiae copulatur' is defective; read as 'particularitas substantiae'. 'subjecta grammatica' taken as grammar being placed under knowledge as a species. 'poteat' read as 'potest'.

passages.original: Ubi enim res discrepant,et definitio discrepabit;ita quoque in his,nam quoniam discrepat substantia et accidens,diffinitiones quoque eorum discrepabunt.Ut quoniam est accidens in subjecto, erit substantia non in subjecto. Et quoniam universalitas de subjecto praedicatur, particularitas autem ab universalitate discrepat,de subjecto non praedicatur. Has igitur hujusmodi descriptiones Aristoteles itapermiscuit dicens : Eorum quae sunt, alia de subjecto quodam diountur, in subjecto vero nullo sunt, volens scilicet universalem substantiam demonstrare. Nam quod dixit de subjecto dicuntur,universaleest, quod vero ait.
passages.english: For where things differ, the definition too will differ; so also in these cases, for since substance and accident differ, their definitions too will differ. Thus, since accident is in a subject, substance will be not in a subject. And since universality is predicated of a subject, while particularity differs from universality, [particularity] is not predicated of a subject. These descriptions of this kind, then, Aristotle combined thus, saying: "Of the things that are, some are said of a certain subject but are in no subject," wishing, namely, to indicate universal substance. For what he said, "are said of a subject", is the universal; but what he said,

passages.original: Igitur universaliter pronuntiat praedicamenta affirmationis ratione penitus non teneri : sed haec eadem si cum quadam complexione conjuncta sint, fieri propositiones necesse est, quae in se verum falsumve contineant. Sed non omnis complexio propositionem facit,nec si dixero, Socrates in foro, idcirco jam propositio est ; sed si quis dicat, Socrates in foro ambulat, tunc fit propositio, quae autaffirmatio est aut negatio. Affirmationesautem et negationes, vel verævidentur esse vel falsae : atque ideo quodcunque neque verum neque falsum est, illud propositio non est.
passages.english: So he states universally that the categories are in no way held by the character of affirmation; but if these same things are joined in some combination, propositions must result, which contain in themselves truth or falsity. But not every combination makes a proposition: if I say, 'Socrates in the forum', that is not yet a proposition; but if someone says, 'Socrates walks in the forum', then a proposition results, which is either an affirmation or a negation. And affirmations and negations seem to be either true or false; and therefore whatever is neither true nor false is not a proposition.

passages.original: Facit autem quamdam sub- stantiarum divisionem cum dicit,alias primas esse substantias, alias secundas : primas vocans individuas,secundas vero individuarum speciesel genera: Ergo cum primis secundisque subtantiis commune sit non esse in subjecto,additum primis substantiis, de subjectis non prædicari, primas substantias a secundis substantiis separat;substantia enim ind ividua, in eo quod est substantia, in subjecto non est: quod autem individua est, de subjecto non prædicatur. Sunt ergo primae substantiæ quae neque in subjecto sunt, neque de subjecto dicuntur, ut est Socrates vel Plato.Hienim quoniam substantiae sunt, in subjecto nullo sunt. Quoniam vero particulares individuique sunt, ne nullo subjecto prædicantur. Secundae vero substantiæ sunt, quibus commune est cum primis substantiis, quod in subjecto non sunt, proprium vero quod de subjecto prædicantur, quae secundae substantiae sunt universales, ut est homo atqueanimal;
passages.english: He makes a certain division of substances when he says that some substances are primary, others secondary, calling the individual ones primary, and the species and genera of the individuals secondary. So, since it is common to primary and secondary substances not to be in a subject, by adding for primary substances that they are not predicated of subjects, he separates primary substances from secondary substances; for individual substance, inasmuch as it is substance, is not in a subject, and inasmuch as it is individual, it is not predicated of a subject. Primary substances, then, are those which are neither in a subject nor said of a subject, such as Socrates or Plato. For these, since they are substances, are in no subject; and since they are particular and individual, they are predicated of no subject. Secondary substances are those which have in common with primary substances that they are not in a subject, but have as their own that they are predicated of a subject; these secondary substances are universal, such as man and animal;
passages.notes: 'ne nullo subjecto' read as 'de nullo subjecto'.

passages.original: Prædictum est quoque,ut Porphyrius in libro de generibus, speciebus, differentiis, propriis, atque accidentibus planissime docuit, alia esse solumgenera,quorum genus inveniri non posset,alia solum species,quae in alias species dividi non valerent.
passages.english: It was also said before, as Porphyry taught most plainly in his book on genera, species, differences, properties and accidents, that some are genera only, of which no genus could be found, and others species only, which could not be divided into other species.

passages.original: Quare secundae substantiæ primas substantias ad prædicationem tantum subjectas habent, non etiam ut ipsae primis substantiis accidant.Illud quoque maximum argu- mentum est secundas substantias non esse in subjecto, quoniam omne quod in subjecto est potest mutari,illa quoe subjecta est non mutatur,ut color qui est in corpore, eodem corpore manente potest mutari,ut niger fiat ex albo.Manentibus autem substantiis primis,secundæ substantias non mutantur. Quam vero ipse Aristoteles posuit probationem,secundas substantias non esse in subjecto,hujusmodi est, prædocuit enim quorumdam quæ sunt in subjecto nomen de subjectis posse prædicari,rationem vero nunquam. Album enim cum sit in corpore,dicitur corpus album,et praedicatur albedo de corpore,sed alia est diffinitio albedinis, alia corporis.
passages.english: Therefore second substances have first substances underlying them only for predication, not so that they themselves are accidents of the first substances. This too is a very strong argument that second substances are not in a subject: everything that is in a subject can change while that which is its subject does not change, as the colour that is in a body can change while the same body remains, so that it becomes black from white. But while first substances remain, second substances do not change. The proof Aristotle himself gave that second substances are not in a subject is of this kind: he taught beforehand that of certain things that are in a subject the name can be predicated of the subjects, but never the definition. For since white is in a body, the body is called white, and whiteness is predicated of the body, but the definition of whiteness is one thing, that of body another.

passages.original: Quoniam in subjecto non esse differentiis et substantiiscommunemonstravit,aliam rursus communitatem substantiarum differentiarumque proposuit.Nam cum substantiarum alix sint primae, aliæ secundæ,et primæ substantiæ sint individuae, quoniam nihil individua possunt habere subjectum,ab individuis nulla prædicatio est.Secundae verosubstantise de individuis, id est de primis substantiis, prædicantur, et de his univoce dicuntur. Secundarum enim substantiarum nomen de individuis prædicatur et ratio. Ac de individuo quidem et species prædicatur et genus,ut de Platone,id est de aliquo homine,ethomo dicitur,et animai,aliquis enim homo est,et animal,et utriusque de individuo praedicatur ratio.Dicimus enim aliquem hominem animal esse rationale mortale, quae est speciei diffinitio, id est hominis.Et rursus aliquem hominem dicimus esse substantiam animatam atque sensibilem,quæ generis est diffinitio,id est animalis.Species vero generis sui et diffinitionem suscipitetvocabulum,de homine emin animal prædicatur,dicitur eniin homo animal est,et idem ipse rursus homo rationem suscipit animalis.Dicimus enim esse hominem substantiam animatam atque sensibilem.
passages.english: Since he has shown that not being in a subject is common to differences and substances, he has set out another thing that substances and differences have in common. For since of substances some are first and others second, and first substances are individuals, since individuals can have nothing as subject, there is no predication from individuals. But second substances are predicated of individuals, that is, of first substances, and are said of them univocally. For both the name and the definition of second substances are predicated of individuals. And of the individual both the species and the genus are predicated, as of Plato, that is, of a certain man, both "man" and "animal" are said, for a certain man is both a man and an animal, and the definition of each is predicated of the individual. For we say that a certain man is a rational mortal animal, which is the definition of the species, that is, of man. And again we say that a certain man is an animate and sensible substance, which is the definition of the genus, that is, of animal. And the species receives both the definition and the name of its genus, for animal is predicated of man, since it is said "man is an animal", and that same man in turn receives the definition of animal. For we say that man is an animate and sensible substance.

passages.original: Constat ergo quoniam et genera et species de individuis,et genera de spe- ciebus univoce praedicantur, id est in omni praedicatione secundae substantiæ univoca appellatione de subjectisdicuntur,quod his cumdifferentiacommune est.Differenlia namque de specie de qua dicitur, etde ejus individuo ipsa quoque univoce prædicatur. Nam cum sit gressibilis differentia de aliquo homine prsedicatur,dicitur enim quidam homo gressibilis, ut Plato et Cicero,sed et diffinitionem differentias suscipiunt individua,de quibus illa differentia praedicatur.Gressibile namque est quod per terram pedibus ambulare potest.Etquemdamhominem possis ita secundum nomen differentiae diffinire, ut dicas Platonem esse quod per terram pedibus ambulare possit.
passages.english: It is clear, then, that both genera and species are predicated univocally of individuals, and genera of species; that is, in every predication second substances are said of their subjects with a univocal appellation, which they have in common with difference. For difference too is itself predicated univocally of the species of which it is said, and of its individual. For since "walking" is a difference, it is predicated of a certain man, for a certain man is called walking, such as Plato and Cicero; but the individuals of which that difference is predicated also receive the definition of the difference. For walking is what can go about on the earth on feet. And you could define a certain man according to the name of the difference in such a way as to say that Plato is what can go about on the earth on feet.

passages.original: Ergo et differentiæ de his de quibus pradicantur,univocedi- cuntur.Quocirca quoniam et secundae substantiæ de his de quibus prædicantur univoce dicuntur,et differentias eodem modo,quæcunque a substantiis vel differentiis praedicationes fuerint,haec et de subjectis univoce prædicabuntur.Quæ autem causa sit ut secundae substantiæ de primis substantiis univoce prædicentur,illa quam supra docuit Aristoteles nos admonens dixit,omnia enim quaecunque de prædicato dicuntur,eadern etiam dicentur de subjecto.Omnes enim difrerentiæ quæ sunt specifica? generis praedicantur et de specie et de individuo, ut quoniam ani- mal efficiunt differentiæ animatum atque sensibile, eadem et de specie, id est homine, et de individuo, id est aliquo homine,prædicabuntur;
passages.english: Therefore differences too are said univocally of those things of which they are predicated. Hence, since both second substances are said univocally of those things of which they are predicated, and differences in the same way, whatever predications come from substances or differences will also be predicated univocally of the subjects. And the reason why second substances are predicated univocally of first substances is the one Aristotle taught above when, reminding us, he said: for whatever things are said of the predicate will also be said of the subject. For all the differences which are specific [differences] of the genus are predicated both of the species and of the individual; thus since the differences "animate" and "sensible" make up animal, these same will be predicated both of the species, that is, man, and of the individual, that is, a certain man;
passages.notes: "specificae" read for "specifica?". The sentence continues in the following context.

passages.original: Quod si hoc est, vel quatuor,vel tres, vel quinque,vel quicunque a duobus distant numeri, contrarii fiant duobus, et erunt uni rei multa contraria, quod fieri non potest.Non est igitur contrarium aliquid quantitati.Sed si quis dicat magnum pravo vel multae paucis esse contraria, haec quidem etiamsi quis quantitates esse confirmat,tamen diffinitæ quantitates non sunt,quantum enim sit magnum vel quantum parvum,non definit qui loquitur, eodem modo, etiam de multis atque paucis. Quare si quis hæc quantitates esse dicat,indeterminatas indefinilasque esse confitebitur.Dicit autem Aristoteles terminatae quantitati nihiiessecontrarium,utduobusveltribus vel lineae vel superficiei.Quod si etiam aliae quantitates habent contraria,aliee vero non habent,nihil omnino impedit ad hoc quod dicitur, proprium non esse substantiæ,idcirco quod constat quasdam quantitates non habere contraria.Quod si hoc et in quantitatibus evenitnon esse contrarium,substantiarum proprium non est.Atque hæc quidem si quis magnum velparvum in quantitatibus ponat, manifestum est (ut ipse est posterius monstraturus) hæc non esse quantitates,sed ad aliquid,magnumenimad parvum dicitur;sed cum ad ea loca venerimus, propositi ordinem loci diligentius exsequemur.Nunc quoniam declaratum est et substantiæ nihil esse contrarium, et hoc ei proprium non esse,quoniam idem etiam in quantitatibus consideratur,ad sequens proprium expositionis semitam convertamus.
passages.english: But if this is so, either four, or three, or five, or whatever numbers differ from two, would become contrary to two, and there would be many contraries to one thing, which cannot happen. Nothing, therefore, is contrary to quantity. But if someone says that large is contrary to small, or many to few, even if someone affirms that these are quantities, still they are not definite quantities, for whoever speaks does not define how much is large or how much small, and likewise with many and few. Therefore if someone says that these are quantities, he will admit that they are indeterminate and indefinite. But Aristotle says that nothing is contrary to a determinate quantity, such as two or three, or a line or a surface. And if some quantities have contraries while others do not, nothing at all prevents what is said, that this is not a property of substance, because it is established that some quantities do not have contraries. And if this too occurs in quantities, that there is no contrary, it is not a property of substances. And as for these, if someone places large or small among quantities, it is clear (as he himself will show later) that these are not quantities but relatives, for large is said in relation to small; but when we come to those places, we will follow out the order of the proposed topic more carefully. Now, since it has been made clear both that nothing is contrary to substance and that this is not its property, since the same is also observed in quantities, let us turn the path of exposition to the next property.
passages.notes: "pravo" read as "parvo".

passages.original: At vero et actio eadem et una numero non erit bona atque mala,sed fortasse una bona, alia mala, ita ut diversae sint,non eaedem numero, hoc etiam in aliis reperitur.Ipsaverosubstantia cum una sit et numero singalaris,contraria suscipil ,ut idem atque unus homo cum fuerit candidus atque albus a sole tactus nigrescit,et album in nigrum convertitur,et i in contrarium permutatur,utrasqueres in se contrarias suscipiens.NuIli igitur alii in esse hoc nisi solis substantiis,satis superiora demonstrant SiquisauteJ3 opponat orationem et opinionem unam atque eamdem contrariorum essesusceptibilem,ideo quod cum dico Cicero sedet,vel eum sedere opinor, cum vere sedet, vera est et oratio de eodem et opinio quod sedet; cum vera surrexit ille,eadem permanet opinio vel oratio quas dicit vel arbitratur Cicero sedet, sed falsa est, quod non sedet, videtur opinio atque oratio eadem et una numero nunc quidem esse vera, nunc autem falsa,et contraria ipsa auscipere,sed hoc falsumest,quodoratioetopiniocontrarianonrecipiunt: nam si quis hoc recipiatquod etiam oratioatqueopinio contrariorum susceptiva sint,non tamen eodem modo quo substantia.Nam substantia ipsa contraria suscipiens permutatur, Cicero namque ipse in se aegritudinem suscipiens ex sano factus est æger,et mutatus ipse contraria suscipit;sermo vero vel opinio ipsa quidem immutata permanent,sed cum rebus de quibus dicuntur permutatis ips£ e inveniuntur falsae esse vel verae.Et substantia quidem ipsa cum iis quae suscipit contrariis permutatur;
passages.english: But likewise an action, the same and one in number, will not be good and bad, but perhaps one good and another bad, so that they are different and not the same in number; this is also found in other cases. But substance itself, while it is one and singular in number, receives contraries; as one and the same man, when he was fair and white, darkens when touched by the sun, and white is turned into black, and it changes into its contrary, receiving both contrary things in itself. That this belongs to nothing else but substances alone, what has gone before shows sufficiently. But if someone objects that speech and opinion, one and the same, are receptive of contraries, because when I say "Cicero is sitting", or think he sits, when he truly sits, both the speech and the opinion about him that he sits are true; when he has got up, the same opinion or speech remains which says or thinks "Cicero is sitting", but it is false, since he is not sitting; thus opinion and speech, the same and one in number, seem now to be true, now false, and to receive contraries themselves. But this is false, because speech and opinion do not receive contraries; for even if someone accepts that speech and opinion too are receptive of contraries, it is still not in the same way as substance. For substance itself, receiving contraries, is changed: Cicero himself, receiving sickness into himself, has become sick from healthy, and being changed himself he receives contraries; but speech or opinion themselves remain unchanged, but when the things of which they are said are changed, they themselves are found to be false or true. And substance itself is changed along with the contraries it receives;
passages.notes: "surrexit ille" read for "vera surrexit ille" ("vera" likely "vero"). The sentence continues in the following context.

passages.original: Quocirca etiam oratio quantitas videtur esse discreta.Sed si quis fortasse dicat hunc eorum esse communem terminum,quo itajunguntur,utaliquid significent,ut in hoc ipso nomine Cicero communis syllabarum terminus ipsa significatio sit.Si enim ce syllaba,quae media est,prima ponatur,etro, quae ultima est,media, et ci,quae prima est,ultima, nomen quoderatantea,idest Cicero, transversis per locasyllabis nihil significabit.Illi dicendum est quoniam quaecunque in quadam oratione proferuntur, sive significent, sive nihil significent, syllabarum communis terminus nullus est. Nam si quis dicat, permutatis syllabis,quod est Cicero,ceroci significationem quidem amisit,sed aequalitersyllabae ad nullum communem terminum conjunguntur. Quod si quis hunc quidem ipsum sermonem aliquid significare posuerit,uthoc ipsumCicero aliquid significat, significatioquidemadditaest,nullus tamen syllabis terminus appositus.
passages.english: Therefore speech too seems to be a discrete quantity. But perhaps someone might say that the common boundary of these [syllables] is that by which they are joined so as to signify something, so that in this very name "Cicero" the common boundary of the syllables would be the signification itself. For if the syllable "ce", which is in the middle, is put first, and "ro", which is last, in the middle, and "ci", which is first, last, the name which existed before, that is, "Cicero", will signify nothing once its syllables have been shifted out of their places. To him it must be said that whatever is uttered in any speech, whether it signifies or signifies nothing, has no common boundary of its syllables. For if someone, with the syllables of "Cicero" rearranged, says "ceroci", it has indeed lost its signification, but the syllables are equally joined at no common boundary. And if someone lays it down that this very utterance signifies something, as "Cicero" itself signifies something, signification has indeed been added, yet no boundary has been attached to the syllables.
passages.notes: Many run-together words from scanning (e.g. 'quoderatantea', 'locasyllabis') silently separated.

passages.original: Mox enim dicitur sermo, mox præterit, nec ulla ratione poterit permanere,quare mox ut aliquid dictum sit, ejus partes ostendi et demonstratione sumi non possunt. Constat igitur orationem quoque ex his esse quae positionem partium non habent,de ordine vero dubium est. Nam si quis sermo aliquid significet, ut est Cicero, est in eo quidam ordo quod ci syllaba primum dicitur,secunda vero ce, tertia ro, et potius ex significatione ordinem sumit; si vero nihil significet,nec ordinem dicitur habere,ut scindapsus nihil quidem significat;
passages.english: For speech is no sooner spoken than it passes away, and can in no way remain; so as soon as something has been said, its parts cannot be pointed out or taken by demonstration. It is established, then, that speech too belongs to those things whose parts have no position; but about order there is doubt. For if an utterance signifies something, as "Cicero" does, there is a certain order in it, in that the syllable "ci" is said first, "ce" second, and "ro" third, and it takes its order rather from its signification; but if it signifies nothing, it is not said to have order either, as "scindapsus" signifies nothing;
passages.notes: 'scindapsus' is a standard example of a meaningless word.

passages.original: neque enim bicubito tricubitum contrarium est,sicut neque numerus ulli numenl,al vero nec superficies soliditati,nec aliquid borum.Sed quoniam quaedam indefinitaimaginem quamdam quantitatisostendunt; ut magnum et parvum,quae videntur esse contraria, hæc sibi Aristoteles opponit dicens non esse quantitates,sed magis ad aliquid, quod ipsius sermonibus astruan:us.Sed non est hoc proprium quantitatis non habere contraria,nonenimomnis quantitas contrariis caret,sed nobis persingula quaaquecurrentibus quae quantitatis species contraria non habeant, quæve habeant,considerandumestLineaquidem contrario caret, linea enim lienaa contraria non est;sed si quis dicatrectamlineamcurvaelineae esse contrariam, fallitur.Non enim in eo quod linea est, curva linea rectae lineae contraria est, sed in eo quod curva est, et in his non lineae videntur esse contrariæ, sed ipsa rectitudo et curvitas.Quarenon in eo quod quantitas est, linea curva rectae lineae contraria est,sed in eo quod qualis.
passages.english: for neither is two-cubits contrary to three-cubits, just as no number is contrary to any number, nor indeed surface to solid, nor anything of these. But since certain indefinite things display a kind of image of quantity, such as large and small, which seem to be contraries, Aristotle sets these against himself, saying that they are not quantities but rather relatives, which we shall establish from his own words. But it is not a property of quantity to have no contraries, for not every quantity lacks contraries; rather we must consider, running through each one, which species of quantity have no contraries, or which have them. A line indeed lacks a contrary, for a line is not contrary to a line; but if someone says that a straight line is contrary to a curved line, he is mistaken. For it is not insofar as it is a line that a curved line is contrary to a straight line, but insofar as it is curved; and in these it is not the lines that seem to be contrary, but straightness and curvature themselves. Therefore it is not insofar as it is a quantity that a curved line is contrary to a straight line, but insofar as it is of a certain quality.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'numenl,al vero' read as 'numero, at vero'; 'borum' as 'horum'; 'lienaa' as 'lineae'; 'astruan:us' as 'astruamus'.

passages.original: cum enim dico dominus,per seipsum nihil est,si servus dicit, Quo- circa cum unius relativi nuncupatio mox secum etiax aliud trahat ad aliquid,unum esse per se non potest, atque ideo non dixit Aristoteles: Ad aliquid verotale dicitur,sed,pluralinumero,talia dicuntur,inquit,demonstrans relativorum intelligentiam non in simplicitate,sed in pluralitate consistere; non esse autem quamdam per se relativorum naturam sine conjunctione aliqua alterius subsistente, ipse Aristoteles monstrat,qui dicit ea esse relativa,quæcu nque hoc ipsum quodsuntaliorum dicuntur.Docetenim aliqua conjunctione alterius relativa formari, hoc ipsum enim quod sunt aliorum dicuntur.Quodenimest dominus,hoc alterius dicitur,id est servi.
passages.english: for when I say "master", it is nothing by itself unless it speaks of a slave. Therefore, since the naming of one relative at once draws another along with it, a relative cannot be one by itself; and for this reason Aristotle did not say "Such a thing is called relative" but, in the plural, "such things are called", showing that the understanding of relatives consists not in singleness but in plurality. And that there is no nature of relatives subsisting by itself without some conjunction with another, Aristotle himself shows, who says that those things are relatives which, just what they are, are said of others. For he teaches that relatives are formed by some conjunction with another, since just what they are is said of others. For what a master is, this is said of another, that is, of a slave.
passages.notes: 'si servus dicit' likely corrupt; perhaps 'nisi servum dicit' or 'si servus desit'; translated as 'unless it speaks of a slave'.

passages.original: Secundum enim has quales dicimur, scientes scilicet atque inscii.Quocirca quoniam praeter aliud praedicamentum per se relativa nullus intelliget,secundum ea praedicamenta de quibus intelligitur relatio,secundumeadiciturcontrariapossesuscipere: ut Socrates ipsequidemsubstantiaest,sed substantia contrarium non recipit. Pater vero atque filius secundum substantiam praedicatur, non est enim pater atque filius nisi in substantia sit. Quocirca quoniam secundum substantiam dicitur, contrarietate caret.Rureuaduplumveldimidium secundum quantitatem dicitur,quantitas vero contraria non habere monstrata est;
passages.english: For according to these we are called qualified, namely knowing and ignorant. Therefore, since no one will understand relatives by themselves apart from another category, relatives are said to be able to admit contraries according to those categories in respect of which the relation is understood. For example, Socrates himself is a substance, but substance does not admit a contrary. Father and son are predicated according to substance, for there is no father or son unless it is in a substance. Therefore, since it is said according to substance, it lacks contrariety. Again, double or half is said according to quantity, and quantity has been shown not to have contraries;

passages.original: Aiunt enim non esse solius relationis ad convertentiam dici Si quis enim sic dicat: cum sol super terram est,dies est,et cum dies est super terram,sol est, recipiunt haec quoque conversionem, quae confessae a relativorum definitione segregata sunt.Non igitur in solis relativis,inquiunt,caditista conversio.Sed Jaroblicusduashujus rei protulit solutiones,unam pervacuam,aliam vero perforem. Ait enim nihil officere ad Aristotelis sententiam, si et alia convertantur; non enim inquit Aristoteles solis hoc relativis esse,sed,omnibus namque hoc relativis inest,nec ulla ratione negari potest: quocirca quoniam non dixiL Aristoteles solis hoc inesse relativis,illorum quæstio hujus praeclari philosophi sententiam non moratur.
passages.english: For they say that being said reciprocally does not belong to relation alone. For if someone says thus: when the sun is above the earth, it is day, and when it is day, the sun is above the earth, these too admit of conversion, though they are admittedly excluded from the definition of relatives. Therefore, they say, this conversion does not occur in relatives alone. But Iamblichus offered two solutions of this matter, one quite empty, the other stronger. For he says it does no harm to Aristotle's view if other things also convert; for Aristotle did not say that this belongs to relatives alone, but [said] "for this belongs to all relatives", and that cannot be denied by any reasoning; therefore, since Aristotle did not say that this belongs to relatives alone, their objection does not hinder the view of this distinguished philosopher.
passages.notes: 'Jaroblicus' read as Iamblichus; 'perforem' read as 'fortiorem' (stronger).

passages.original: Non igitur sicut sensibilis interemptio sensus interimit,sic sensuum perditionem exstinctio sensibilium comitatur.Id vero etiam hoc probabitur argumento, anteenim quam actu ipso aliquid sentiamus, sensus non est.Nam priusquam dulce aliquid degustemus, gustatio ipsa dulcedinis non est; quod autemgustari possit,id est, mel,vel quodlibet aliud propriæ naturae ratione consistit. Quocirca prius esse quod sentiri possit,post vero sensus Aristotele auctore firmatur.
passages.english: Therefore, just as the destruction of the sensible destroys the senses, so the extinction of the sensibles does not... rather: it is not the case that, just as the destruction of the sensible destroys sense, so the loss of the senses accompanies the extinction of sensibles. This will also be proved by this argument: before we actually perceive something, sense does not exist. For before we taste something sweet, the tasting of sweetness does not exist; but what can be tasted, that is, honey or anything else, subsists by the account of its own nature. Therefore, on Aristotle's authority, it is established that what can be perceived exists first, and sense afterward.
passages.notes: The first sentence is logically odd as transmitted (one expects 'the destruction of sense does not destroy the sensible'); the text may be corrupt. Literal sense: 'Not, then, as the destruction of the sensible destroys sense, so does the extinction of sensibles accompany the loss of the senses.'

passages.original: aut enim diffinitio relativorum reprehendenda est,aut aliter solvenda dubie- tas.Sed posita atque constituta priori diffinitione, quae dicit illa esse relativa quæ id quod sunt aliorum dicuntur,hic quaestionis nodus solvi non poterit,quod ipse Aristoteles hac adjunctione testatur.
passages.english: for either the definition of relatives must be faulted, or the doubt must be resolved in another way. But with the earlier definition laid down and established, which says that those things are relatives which are said, just what they are, of others, this knot of the question cannot be untied, as Aristotle himself attests by this addition.

passages.original: Proponit qualitatem multipliciter dici, quae res traxit aliquos in errorem, ut eis suspicio nasceretur Aristotelem credere qualitatem aequivoce nominari. Nam si omnisaequivocatio multipliciter dicitur,qua- litas autem secundum Aristotelem ipsa quoque multipliciter appellatur, secundum Aristotelem nomen qualitatisaequivocum est. Nos vero defendimus multipliciter dici, esse non una tantum significatione nominari. Dicitur enim aliquid multipliciter dici, cum et aequivoce dicitur, et diverso modo de suis speciebus multipliciter praedicatur.Etcommunisest multiplex appellatio, etiam in bis nominibus quae veluti genera de speciebus dicuntr, velut aequivoca desubjectis.Namqueetanimal multipliciterdicitur.
passages.english: He states that quality is spoken of in many ways, a point which has led some into error, so that the suspicion arose in them that Aristotle believed quality is named equivocally. For if every equivocation is spoken of in many ways, and quality too, according to Aristotle, is itself called so in many ways, then according to Aristotle the name 'quality' is equivocal. But we maintain that to be spoken of in many ways is to be named not with one meaning only. For something is said to be spoken of in many ways both when it is said equivocally and when it is predicated in different ways of its species. And the manifold appellation is common also to those names which are said of their species as genera, just as equivocals are said of their subjects. For 'animal' too is spoken of in many ways.
passages.notes: "esse non una tantum significatione nominari" is syntactically loose; rendered by sense.

passages.original: Reliquum est ;igiturea nequegenere neque specie differre, sed numero. Habitus namque dispositio idem est secundum speciem, sed numero tantum et propria quadam qualitate dissentiunt. Dispositionem vero indiscrete idem quod affectionem voco. Nam sicut Socrates a Platone nihil quidem secundum ipsam humanitatis speciem discrepat, sola tamen propriae personæ qualitate disjuncti sunt, ita quoque dispositio atque habitus, nee potius hoc modo distant; sed quemadmodum ipse Socrates dum esset parvulus, post vero pubescens a seipso distabat, eodem quoque modo habitus etdispositio : namque habitus firma est dispositio, affectio infirmus est habitus, ut quemadmodum distat albus color ab albo colore, si in pictura hic quidem permaneat, ille vero statim periturus sit, nisi quod is qui permanentior est, in habitu est, ille vero qui facile periturus est, in affectione, ita nihil aliud interest inter habitum atque dispositionem.
passages.english: It remains, therefore, that they differ neither in genus nor in species, but in number. For state and disposition are the same in species, but differ only in number and by a certain proper quality. And I call disposition indiscriminately the same as affection. For just as Socrates differs in no way from Plato in the very species of humanity, yet they are separated solely by the quality of their own person, so too disposition and state; or rather, they do not differ in this way, but just as Socrates himself, when he was a small child and afterwards as a youth, differed from himself, so likewise state and disposition. For a state is a firm disposition, and an affection is an infirm state; so that just as white colour differs from white colour, if in a painting one remains while the other is about to perish at once, except that the one which is more lasting is in [the condition of] a state, while the one that will easily perish is in [the condition of] an affection, so there is no other difference between state and disposition.
passages.notes: 'nee potius hoc modo distant' read as 'nec potius'; the sense of the sentence is somewhat awkward. 'habitus' rendered 'state'.

passages.original: Quocirca sive per aegritudinem pallor fit,quod naturale non rst, sive per aliquem naturalem eventum passiunis accidat, cæteraque ad eumdem modum, passibiles qualitates di- cuntur,eo quod ex aliquibus passionibus sint,quod ipse Aristoteles hac voce testatur : I
passages.english: Therefore, whether pallor arises through illness, which is not natural, or occurs through some natural event of affection, and the rest in the same way, they are called affective qualities, because they arise from certain affections, as Aristotle himself attests in these words:
passages.notes: Passage ends with the quotation cut off.

passages.original: namque et dispositionem dixit calorem atque frigus, et passibilem qualitatem.Hujus quaestionis talis solutio est. Nihil impedit,secundum aliam scilicet atque aliam causam, unam eamdemque rem gemino generi speciei suae supponere,ut Socrates in eo quod pater est ad aliquid dicitur,in eo quod homo, substantia est,sic in calore atque frigore, in eo quod quis secundum ea videtur esse dispositus, in dispositione numerata sunt; secundum vero quod ex aliquibus passionibus innascuntur,passibiles qualitates dictae sunt.
passages.english: for he called heat and cold both a disposition and an affective quality. The solution of this question is as follows. Nothing prevents one and the same thing, by reason of one cause and another, from being placed under two genera as its species: just as Socrates, in that he is a father, is said [to be] relative, and in that he is a man, is a substance, so heat and cold, insofar as someone seems to be disposed according to them, are counted under disposition; but insofar as they arise from certain affections, they are called affective qualities.

passages.original: Idcirco quod hae qualitates a quibus denominari possunt, propriis nominibus carent, quæ vero ita sint, ut non ex potentia, sed ex affectione dicantur,ab his qualitatibas ad quas sese aliquomodohabent,deno- minative dicuntur, quod Aristoteles hoc protulit modo dicens : Non ita esse secundum potentiam naturalem, quemadmodum etiam in disciplinis secundum quas, vel pugillatores,vel palæstrici secundum affectionemdicuntur.Pugillatoriaenimdisciplinadicitur et palæstrica,quales vero ab his denominative, qui ad eas sunt continentes, dicuntur.Docuit igitur omnia quæ a quibusdam qualitatibus dici putarentur, vero quoque a qualitatibus non prædicari,ut in his qualitatibus quibus nomen proprium non est.Illud quoque monstravit hoc in pluribus evenire, ut de propositis qualitatibusqualiadenominativedicerentur.
passages.english: [This is] because these qualities from which they could be named lack proper names; but those which are such that they are spoken of not from capacity but from disposition are named denominatively from the qualities to which they are in some way related, which Aristotle put in this manner, saying: "It is not so in the case of natural capacity as in the disciplines according to which people are called boxers or wrestlers according to a disposition." For there is said to be a discipline of boxing and of wrestling, while those who are disposed toward them are called such-and-such denominatively from them. He taught, then, that all the things thought to be named from certain qualities are not in fact predicated from qualities, as in those qualities which have no proper name. He also showed this, that in most cases it happens that things are called such-and-such denominatively from the qualities proposed.
passages.notes: 'vero quoque' probably corrupt (perhaps 'vere non'); rendered as 'in fact'.

passages.original: Quidam vero in hoc dubitant.dicuntenim justitiam justitia non magis vel minus dici,nec sanitatem sa- nitatejminus autem habere alterum altero sanitatem dicunt,et justitiam minus alterum altero habere.In hoc tres fuere sententias.Quidam namque dicebant, in omnibus secundum materiæ habitudinem reperiri posse magis et minus,Proprium namque esse materiae corporumque intentione crescere et minui relaxatione.quae quorumdam Platonicorum sententia fuit.Aliavero quaesecunaum certissimas verissimasque artes atque virtutes non diceret esse magis et minua,secundum autem medias dici posse,ut haec ipsa grammatica atque justitia non dicitur magis grammatica neque magis justitia. Esse autem quasdam alias mediocres artes,in quibusidipsum posset evenire. Tertia est de qua Aristoteles loquitur, quod ipsas quidem habitudinesnullaintentione crescere, nec diminutione decrescere putat,sed eorum participantes posse sub examine compositionis venire,ut de his magis minusve dicatur. Sanitatem namque ipsam al justitiam, alteram altera magis minusve non esse.
passages.english: But some are in doubt on this point. For they say that justice is not called more or less justice than [another] justice, nor health than health; but they say that one person has less health than another, and one has less justice than another. On this there were three opinions. Some said that more and less can be found in all things according to the disposition of the matter, for it is proper to matter and bodies to grow by intensification and diminish by relaxation; this was the opinion of certain Platonists. Another [opinion] said that according to the most certain and truest arts and virtues there is no more and less, but according to the intermediate ones it can be said, as this very grammar and justice is not called more grammar or more justice; but that there are certain other middling arts in which this very thing could occur. The third is the one of which Aristotle speaks, that he thinks the dispositions themselves do not grow by any intensification nor decrease by diminution, but that those who participate in them can come under the scrutiny of comparison, so that more or less is said of them. For health itself or justice is not one more or less than another.

passages.original: Namque ipsa grammatica,id est litteratura,non suscipit magis et minus,nullus enim dicit alteram altera magis esse grammaticam, sed eum qui grammatica ipsa participat. Decimus litteratum,quem a litteratura scilicet denominamus lilte- ratus autem suscipit magis et minus, ut Donatus grammaticus plus erat aetate jam provecta grammaticus,id est litteratus,quam cum primum ad hujusmodi studia devenisset. Sed quanquam se haec ita habeant,tamen invenimus aliquas qualitates quibus indubitate comparatio inveniri non possit, ut sunt quas ipse supposuit.
passages.english: For grammar itself, that is, literacy, does not admit more and less; for no one says that one [grammar] is more grammar than another, but [says this of] the one who participates in grammar. We say [someone is] lettered, whom we name, of course, from literacy; and the lettered person admits more and less, as Donatus the grammarian was more a grammarian, that is, lettered, at an advanced age than when he first came to studies of this kind. But although these things are so, we nevertheless find some qualities in which comparison indubitably cannot be found, such as those which he himself has set down.
passages.notes: 'Decimus' read as 'Dicimus'.

passages.original: Rursus si certa res in tempore est,quando esse perhibetur,ut Apollinares ludi,cum sint. in tempore, quando eos esse dicimus. Habent autem haec quoque proprias diversitates,ubi quidem,quod aliquoties infinite dicitur.Alicubienirr: esse dicimus aliquem,ut Socratem,aliquotiesautem diffinite,ut in lyceo vel in academia. Habet quoque ubi,secundum ipsum locum in quoest,aliquascontrarietates.Sursum enim esse,et deorsum ubi esse dicitur. Temporum quoque varietates in eo praedicamento,quod est quando,esse manifestum est.Futuraenimet praesentia praeteritaque in quando praedicamento veniunt.Dicimus enim fuisse aliquando Scipionem consulem Romanum,nunc esse Orientis imperalorem,qui nunc Anastasius appellatur.Futurum autem esse aliquem, quae scilicet secundum quando praedicamentum dicuntur.
passages.english: Again, if a certain thing is in time, it is said to be 'when', as the Apollinarian games, since they are in time, we say are 'when'. These too have their own varieties: 'where' is sometimes said indefinitely, for we say someone, such as Socrates, is somewhere; but sometimes definitely, as in the Lyceum or in the Academy. 'Where' also has certain contrarieties according to the very place in which [a thing] is: for being above and below is called 'where'. It is also clear that there are varieties of times in the category 'when'. For future, present and past fall into the category 'when'. For we say that Scipio was once Roman consul, that there is now an emperor of the East, who is now called Anastasius; and that someone will be in the future, which are said according to the category 'when'.
passages.notes: The last sentence is elliptical; translated as it stands.

passages.original: Expeditis omnibus prædicamentis,cur præter propositum operis in hanc oppositorum disputationem sit ingressus, a multis ante quaesitum est, sed Andronicus hanc esse adjectionem Aristotelis non putat, simulque illud arbitratur, idcirco ab eo fortasse hanc adjectionem de oppositis,et de his quae simul sunt,et de priore,et de motu et de æquivocatione,habendi non esse factam,quod hunclibellum ante Topica scripserit, quodque haec ad illud opus non necessariaesse putaverit, sicut ipse Categoriae possunt ad sensum Topicorum, non ignorans scilicet quod sufficienter in Topicis,quantumad argumenta pertinebat, et de his omnibus quae adjecta sunt,etdepraedicamentis fuisse propositum.Sed hæc Andronicus.Porphyrius vero hanc adjectionem vacare et carere ratione non putat.Cujus hanc prodidit causam.
passages.english: All the categories having been dealt with, why he entered on this discussion of opposites, beyond the plan of the work, has been asked by many before. Andronicus does not think this addition is Aristotle's, and at the same time he judges that perhaps this addition on opposites, on things simultaneous, on prior, on motion and on the equivocation of 'having' was not made by him because he wrote this little book before the Topics, and thought these things were not necessary for that work, just as the Categories themselves can [serve] for the understanding of the Topics, being well aware that in the Topics, as far as concerned arguments, enough had been set forth both about all these things that are added and about the categories. But so much for Andronicus. Porphyry, however, does not think this addition is idle and lacking in reason, and he gave this cause for it.
passages.notes: The clause 'sicut ipse Categoriae possunt ad sensum Topicorum' is defective and its sense uncertain.

passages.original: Hic ergo contenditur utrum aequivocatio quaedam circa has quatuor diversitates sit, an idipsum quod dicimus oppositum generis vice prædicetur,ut situnivocum.Sed in hoc Stoicorum Peripateticorumque diversa sententia fuit,et ut ipsi inter se Peripatetici,diverse sectati sunt.Stoicorum quoniam longa sententia est,praetermittatur,aliis autem Peripateticis placet nomen hoc oppositi de subjectis aequivoce praedicari,ita affirmantibus,quoniam Aristoteles ita dixit: De oppositis quoties solent opponi dicendum est hoc, id est quoties ad multiplicitatem pertinet aequivocationis.Sed qui meliusjudicavere, hi oppositionis nomen generis loco dicunt debere praedicari, idcirco quod cum nomen opposilionis de subjectis quatuor oppositionibus praedicetur, ab his quoque diffinitio non oberret.
passages.english: Here, then, the question is argued whether there is some equivocation concerning these four kinds of difference, or whether the very thing we call "opposite" is predicated in the manner of a genus, so as to be univocal. But on this the Stoics and the Peripatetics held different views, and the Peripatetics themselves also followed different views among themselves. Since the view of the Stoics is long, let it be passed over. Other Peripatetics, however, hold that this name "opposite" is predicated equivocally of the things under it, affirming this because Aristotle said thus: "Concerning opposites, in how many ways they are customarily opposed, this must be said," that is, in how many ways [the term] belongs to the multiplicity of equivocation. But those who judged better say that the name "opposition" ought to be predicated in the place of a genus, for the reason that, since the name "opposition" is predicated of the four oppositions under it, the definition too does not stray from them.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'situnivocum' = 'sit univocum', 'opposilionis' = 'oppositionis'). The quoted Aristotelian phrase 'quoties' implies 'in how many ways'.

passages.original: Videmus namque rubrum corpus, ut rosam multosque praeterea f1ores,quos verni temporisclementia parturit.Recte igitur dictum est,eorum quorum non sunt aliquae medietates, alterum semper inesse subjectis, et in quibus necesse est alterum inesse,fieri non posse quin illic medietas ulla sit.Eodem quoque modo et quae medietates habent, non cecessario alterutra subjectis inesse,et quae non est necesse alterutra subjectis inesse,non est dubium quin illic quaedam possit esse medietas,sed in aliquibus quidam plures,in aliquibus autem una est medietas, ut in colore inter album alque nigrum plures medietates sunt.Est enim(utdictum est)rubrum, et quoque pallidum,eodem quoque modo venetum, et multa praeterea hujusmodi.In calido vero atque frigido una medietas est,qua3 dicitur tepor.Horum autem quibus una medietas est,in aliis nomen est positum,in allis non.Et positum quidem nomen est, utintercalidum frigidumque,hancenim medietatem tepidum esse praedicamus.Non est vero positum in eo quod Aristoteles ipse sic dixit:Improbi vero et probi, quod neque probum est, neque improbum. Nam quoniam bonum atque malum sibi sunt contraria, non autem necesse est omne quod boni malive susceptibile est,vel bonum esse vel malum,idcirco dixit bonum malumque,cum sintcontraria,babere quamdam medietatem,cui nomen positum quidem non sit,sed nihilominus eam quis inter bas contrariorum naturas inveniet.
passages.english: For we see a red body, such as the rose and many other flowers besides, which the mildness of springtime brings forth. It was rightly said, therefore, that of those [contraries] which have no intermediates, one or the other is always present in the subjects, and that in those in which one of them must be present, it cannot be that there is any intermediate there. In the same way, too, those which have intermediates are not necessarily such that one or the other is present in the subjects, and where it is not necessary that one or the other be present in the subjects, there is no doubt that some intermediate can exist there; but in some there are several, in others only one intermediate, as in colour there are several intermediates between white and black. For there is (as has been said) red, and also pale, likewise blue, and many others of this kind besides. But in hot and cold there is one intermediate, which is called warmth. Of those, however, that have one intermediate, in some a name has been assigned, in others not. A name has been assigned, for instance, between hot and cold, for we call this intermediate lukewarm. But [a name] has not been assigned in the case of which Aristotle himself spoke thus: "Of the bad and the good, what is neither good nor bad." For since good and bad are contrary to each other, yet it is not necessary that everything capable of receiving good or bad be either good or bad, he therefore said that good and bad, though they are contraries, have a certain intermediate to which no name has been assigned, but which one will nonetheless find between these natures of the contraries.
passages.notes: 'venetum' may denote blue or blue-green. 'improbi/probi' rendered 'bad/good'.

passages.original: Quod si distatis qui habet eo ipso quod est habitum habere, distat et is qui privatur eo quod est priva ri.Quod sietiamdistatquod est habereha- bitumillo ipso habitu qui habetur.Distat necessario j id quod est privati illa ipsa scilicet privatione qua quisque privatur.Quare nequeid quod sub habitu est habitus appellari potest,neque id quod sub privatione privatio. Recte igitur dictum est habitum habere non essehabitum,privariquenon esse privationem : cui rei aliqua quaedam validior vis argumentationis adjungitur, quam Aristoteles ita pronuntiat.
passages.english: But if the one who has differs from the very having of a state, the one who is deprived also differs from being deprived. And if, further, having a state differs from the very state that is had, then necessarily being deprived differs from that very privation, namely, by which each is deprived. Therefore neither can that which falls under a state be called a state, nor that which falls under a privation a privation. It was rightly said, then, that having a state is not a state, and being deprived is not a privation; to which a certain stronger force of argument is added, which Aristotle expresses thus.
passages.notes: The first clause 'distatis qui habet' is read as 'distat is qui habet'. 'habitus' rendered 'state' (Aristotle's hexis).

passages.original: Sub negatione vero non sedere Socratem, id est non facere id quod negatiosubmovet.Hocautem ita probatur, quod omnis affirmatio omnisque negatio oraticnes sunt,sicut eorum supradicta diffinitio determinatioque monstravit.Sedere autem et non sedere, id est facere et non facere, orationes non sunt, quod si affirmatio et negatio orationessunt,dicitur id quod sub affirmatione et negatione est,ea ipsa affirmatione et negatione distare.Sed in hoc servant illam quoque similitudinem quod eaipsa sim sunt opposita, quae secundum affirmationem negationemque dicuntur. Sicut enim ipsa affirmatio quae dicit, sedet Socrates, et quai dicit, non sedet Socrates, ita quoque idipsum quod est sedere Socratem, et non sedere, certa ratione similitudinisopponuntur.Sed quoniam quatuor species oppositionis dictae sunt, nunc Aristotelis vestigia persequentes,earum diffe.
passages.english: Under the negation, however, [is] Socrates' not sitting, that is, not doing what the negation removes. This is proved as follows: every affirmation and every negation are statements, as their definition and determination given above showed. But sitting and not sitting, that is, doing and not doing, are not statements; so if affirmation and negation are statements, what is under affirmation and negation is said to differ from that very affirmation and negation. But in this they also preserve that likeness, that these things are opposed in the same way as those said according to affirmation and negation. For just as the affirmation which says 'Socrates sits' and the one which says 'Socrates does not sit' [are opposed], so too Socrates' sitting and not sitting are opposed by a definite relation of likeness. But since four species of opposition have been named, let us now, following in Aristotle's footsteps, gather their differences,
passages.notes: 'eaipsa sim sunt opposita' read as 'eo ipso modo sunt opposita' (in the same way); uncertain.

passages.original: Jam vero illud verum est, ex bono proclivior semper semita videtur ad malum, et facillima esse exprobitate admalitiampermutatio, quod Terentiano docetur exemplo: A labore proclivom ad libidinem.Sed quanquam difficilis sit transitus ad virtutes a turpitudine vitiorum,Aristoteles tamen fieri posse hunc transitum confirmat.Hujua enim philosopbi sententia est, virtutes non esse scientias,ut Socrates ait,neque ut Stoici naturaliter eas esse,sed discibiles, et per quamdam boni consueludinem hominum mentibus inseriri.Atque ideo si quis sit quibuslibet prioribus vitiis obnoxius, si eum melior sermo susceperit,etsapientium consue- tudine confabulationeque comatur,aliquid ex ante actis vitiorum illecebris emendabitur, et sese aliquantulum exuet, et paululum liberior ad meliora procedet.Ita ut sit primo quidem minus malus, post vero non malus, deinde jam jamque aliquantulum bonus.Cuisi hujusmodiintensiofrequentissimefiat, nec parvitate temporis præveniatur,aut ei terminus mortis offecerit, non est dubium illum ex pessimo perprobasconsuetudiDesconfabulationesquesapientum,in perfectam virtutis habitudinem permutari.
passages.english: Now this indeed is true: the path from good to evil always seems more downhill, and the change from uprightness to wickedness is the easiest, as is taught by the example from Terence: "From toil [it is] downhill to lust." But although the passage to the virtues from the baseness of the vices is difficult, Aristotle nevertheless affirms that this passage can take place. For it is the view of this philosopher that the virtues are not sciences, as Socrates says, nor, as the Stoics [say], that they exist by nature, but that they are teachable and are implanted in men's minds through a certain habituation in the good. And therefore, if someone is liable to any former vices whatever, if better discourse takes hold of him, and he is cultivated by the company and conversation of the wise, he will be amended somewhat from the allurements of the vices he previously practised, and will strip himself of them a little, and will advance a little freer toward better things. So that he is at first less bad, then afterwards not bad, and then by and by somewhat good. If an intensification of this kind happens very frequently to him, and is not cut short by brevity of time, or [if] the end of death has not hindered him, there is no doubt that he will be changed from the worst [state], through good habits and the conversations of the wise, into the perfect condition of virtue.
passages.notes: The Terence line (Andria 78) is quoted as "A labore proclivom ad libidinem". "exprobitate admalitiampermutatio" is read as "ex probitate ad malitiam permutatio", and "perprobasconsuetudiDesconfabulationesque" as "per probas consuetudines confabulationesque". "comatur" is probably for "colatur" ("is cultivated"). "offecerit" is taken as "has hindered"; the construction of the "aut" clause is loose.

passages.original: Expositis his differentiis quibus vel contrariis relativa, vel privatio et habitus relativis, vel rursus privatio et habitus contrariis discreparent.,nunc sequitur quid his omnibus secundum affirmationem negationemque opposita distent,et dat signum pro- prium affirmationis et negationis, ut eas semper quæramus agnoscere,ut si qua sint quae hoc signo minime teneantur, ilia ab affirmationis negationisque oppositione differre dicamus.In affirmatione enim et negatione fieri non potest, ut si affirmatio vera sit, statim falsa negatio non sit; si negatio vera, aftirmatio mendacii nota carere possit,ut si quis dicat, Socrates ambulat, Socrates non ambulat. Si verum est Socratem ambulare,falsum est non ambulare, et rursus siverum est non ambulare,falsum est ambulare.Elanc autem veri falsique divisionem nullus unquam in aliis opp ositionibus poterit invenire.Namin his quai sunt ad aliquid non solum non est necesse oppositionem ipsam sibi verum falsumque dividere,sed in his nulla omnino neque veritas, neque falsitas invenitur.Si quis enim dicat hoc tantum, pater, vel rursus,filius, neque verum aliquid neque falsum pronuntiat.
passages.english: Having set out these differences by which relatives differ from contraries, or privation and possession from relatives, or again privation and possession from contraries, it now follows [to show] how all these differ from things opposed as affirmation and negation. He also gives a mark proper to affirmation and negation, so that we may always seek to recognise them, and so that, if there are any things that are not held by this mark, we may say that they differ from the opposition of affirmation and negation. For in affirmation and negation it cannot happen that, if the affirmation is true, the negation is not at once false, or that, if the negation is true, the affirmation can escape the mark of falsehood. For example, if someone says "Socrates walks" and "Socrates does not walk": if it is true that Socrates walks, it is false that he does not walk; and again, if it is true that he does not walk, it is false that he walks. But no one will ever be able to find this division of true and false in the other oppositions. For in relatives, not only is it not necessary that the opposition itself divide true and false between its members, but in them no truth or falsity at all is found. For if someone says only this, "father", or again "son", he states nothing either true or false.

passages.original: Quoniam videntur quædam contraria secundum complexionem dici,in quibus aut falsitas reperitur aut veritas, sed neque ut affirmatio sit neque ut negatio,de his quoque dicit, quid distent his complexionibus, quae secundum affirmationem negationemque dicuntur. Nam sicut aegritudo est contraria sanitati, ita quoque aegrotum esse Socratem, ei quod est sanum esse contrarium est. Oratio quoque quae dicit Socrates sanus est, contraria est ei quae pronuntiat Socrates aegrotat. In his ergo et veritas invenituret falsitas.Quod igitur haec distant ea oppositione quae secundum vim affirmationis aut negationis opponitur,boc scilicet quod subsistente re,de qua utraque dicuntur,utrumlibet eorum verum est, si tamen ea contraria praedicantur,quae mediis carent, nam vivente et subsistente Socrate,quoniam aegritudo et sanitas immediata contraria sunt,si quis de Socrate dicat: Socrates sanus est, rursusque alius pronuntiet: Socrates cegrotat, unam veram, unam falsam esse necesse est.
passages.english: Since certain contraries seem to be said in combination, and in these either falsity or truth is found, yet not in the manner of affirmation or negation, he speaks about these too: how they differ from those combinations that are said by way of affirmation and negation. For just as sickness is contrary to health, so also "that Socrates is sick" is contrary to "that [he] is healthy". The statement too that says "Socrates is healthy" is contrary to the one that declares "Socrates is sick". In these, then, both truth and falsity are found. How, then, these differ from the opposition that is opposed by the force of affirmation or negation [is] this: when the thing of which both are said exists, either one of them is true, provided that the contraries predicated are those that lack intermediates. For while Socrates is alive and exists, since sickness and health are contraries without an intermediate, if someone says of Socrates "Socrates is healthy", and another in turn declares "Socrates is sick", one must be true and one false.
passages.notes: The sentence beginning "Quod igitur haec distant" is syntactically loose; it is rendered by sense.

passages.original: 6i negationes verae sunt, falsae sunt affirmationes. Si vero res subjecta non subsistat omnino, de ea quidem affirmatio falsa est, negatio semper vera. Nostro enim tempore cum Socrates non est ne- que subsistit, si quis dicat Socrates videt, et alius dicat Socrates non videt, laisum quidem est de eo dicere, quoniam videt, verum autem quoniam non videt. Qui enim omnino non est, videre non potest,qui videre non potest,non videt.
passages.english: If the negations are true, the affirmations are false. But if the underlying thing does not exist at all, the affirmation about it is false, [and] the negation always true. For in our time, since Socrates is not and does not exist, if someone says "Socrates sees" and another says "Socrates does not see", it is false to say of him that he sees, but true that he does not see. For one who does not exist at all cannot see, [and] one who cannot see does not see.
passages.notes: "6i" is read as "Si", and "laisum" as "falsum".

passages.original: Si enim nullus aegrotet et sint omnes sani, cum sit sanitas, non erit ægritudo,et una contranetate manente, alia omnino non ent, ut si quis hoc idem dicat de cygnis, etenim omnes cygni sunt albi, in cygnis nigredo non erit.Atque hoc idem ad universalia referendum est.Nam si omnia quae sunt alba sunt, omnino nigredo non erit. Tractum autem hoc videturessesigillatimapartibus.Nam quod duo contraria in eodem uno eodemque tempore esse non possunl,ut Socrates cum sanus est,ægrotus non est, et cum sanus est, manente sanitate, non esse poterit aegritudo. Et non erit necessarium uno contrario posito,moxsubsequi alterum. Nam si necesse esset uno contrario constituto, mox aliquid sequi,posset idem Socrates uno eodemque tempore, et sanus esse et aeger, quod fieri non potest.
passages.english: For if no one is sick and all are healthy, then since there is health, there will be no sickness, and while one contrariety remains, the other will not exist at all. It is the same if someone says this about swans: for if all swans are white, there will be no blackness in swans. And this same point is to be applied to universals. For if all things that exist are white, there will be no blackness at all. This seems to have been drawn, one by one, from the parts. For two contraries cannot be in one and the same [thing] at the same time: for example, Socrates, when he is healthy, is not sick, and when he is healthy, while the health remains, sickness cannot exist [in him]. And it will not be necessary, when one contrary is posited, that the other follow at once. For if it were necessary that, when one contrary is established, something should follow at once, the same Socrates could be both healthy and sick at one and the same time, which cannot happen.
passages.notes: "Tractum ... sigillatim a partibus" ("drawn one by one from the parts") is obscure; it seems to mean that the general claim is reached by induction from particular cases. In the sentence beginning "Nam quod duo contraria", the "quod" has no main verb; it is rendered by sense.

passages.original: Seniorem namque dicimus Pytbagoram Socrate, Socratem Aristotele,idcirco quod se temporibusantecedant.Ergoprius alterum altero dicitur proprie secundum tempus, prioris autem quatuor fuere distantiae, ut ipse Aristoteles dicit, cum ait:Priusalterum altero dicitur quadrupliciter. Easque sigillatim breviter enumerat, ad quas ipse addidit quintam, quae priscis philosophis esset incognita. Et quoniam de primo prioris modo dictum est, de secundo dicemus.
passages.english: For we call Pythagoras older than Socrates, and Socrates than Aristotle, because they precede one another in time. Therefore one thing is properly said to be prior to another according to time. But there were four distinctions of the prior, as Aristotle himself says when he states: "One thing is said to be prior to another in four ways." And he enumerates them briefly one by one, and to them he himself added a fifth, which was unknown to the ancient philosophers. And since the first mode of the prior has been discussed, we shall speak of the second.

passages.original: Ait enim id esse prius inter ea quae convertuntursecundumessentiaeconsequentiam,quod alterius quomodolibet causa est. Ut in hoc ipso sermone de homine,convertuntur utraque quidem,sed homo ut sit sermo verus, causa est atquo principium. Quod Aristoteles ita ait : Est autem verus sermo nullo modo causa subsistendi rem.Res autem videtur quodammodo causa esse ut sermo verus sit. Neque enim idcirco res est, quoniam sermo est, sed idcirco verus est sermo, quoniam res ipsa subsistit.
passages.english: For he says that, among things that reciprocate according to implication of being, that one is prior which is in some way the cause of the other. As in this very case of the statement about a man: both reciprocate, but the man is the cause and principle of the statement's being true. Which Aristotle states thus: "The true statement is in no way the cause of the thing's existing; but the thing seems in some way to be the cause of the statement's being true." For the thing does not exist because the statement exists, but the statement is true because the thing itself exists.

passages.original: ut prius aliquis sit pater, post vero (ilius.Mox enim ut pater est, filium esse necesse est, mox ut est filius, patris sine dubio praedicatio consequitur, ■ quemadmodum ergo iste modus fit, qui scilicet simul secundum naturam est, Aristoteles ita pronuntiat.
passages.english: so that someone is first a father and afterwards a son. For as soon as there is a father, there must be a son; as soon as there is a son, the predication of father undoubtedly follows. How, then, this mode comes about, namely the one which is simultaneous by nature, Aristotle states thus.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the preceding context implies a negation ('it is not the case that someone is first a father...'). 'post vero (ilius' read as 'filius'.

passages.original: Dividatur enim genus,idest animali in volatile atquegressibile, et quoniam sunt sub eodem genere, simul natura sunt.Et si quid horum in subjectas partes speciesque solvatur, ut volatile quidem in his avibus quae seminibus vescuntur,et in iis quaecarnibus,etin his quae herbis,hae tres species rursus,quae sub volatili sunt, simul esse naturaliterappellantur,quod Aristoteles ita dicit.
passages.english: For let a genus, that is, animal, be divided into winged and walking; and since these are under the same genus, they are simultaneous by nature. And if any of these is broken up into subordinate parts and species, as winged into those birds which feed on seeds, those which [feed] on flesh, and those which [feed] on grasses, these three species in turn, which are under winged, are called simultaneous by nature; which Aristotle says thus.

passages.original: In commutatione veroestaliqua dubitatio,ne forte necesse sit quod commutatur secundum aliquem reliquorum motuum commutari.Namsi omne quod commutatur, aut generatur, aut corrumpitur, aut minuitur, aut crescit, aut id secundum locum transferri necesse est, dubium non est nihil a superioribus caeteris hanc differe speciem, quae secundum commutationem dicitur ; quod Aristoteles respuit, dicens, Hoc autem non est verum. Sed quoniam quod commutatur non omnino neque generatur, neque corrumpitur: ut qui in sole diutius stetit,8i ex candido niger est factus, commutatus quidem secundum colorem dicitur, non tamen generatus est aut corruptus, nec vero illi aliquod vel crementum factum est vel diminutio, sed nec loci translatio nulla est, potest enim aliquis uno eodemque loco consistens, aliquibus extrinsecus venientibus passionibus permutari, potest quoque et crescereet decrescere, praeter qualitatis commutationem:quod ipse Aristoteles ita pronuntiat.
passages.english: But regarding alteration there is some doubt, lest perhaps what is altered must be altered according to some one of the remaining motions. For if everything that is altered must either come to be, or perish, or decrease, or increase, or be moved in place, there is no doubt that this species, which is called alteration, does not differ at all from the other ones above; which Aristotle rejects, saying, "But this is not true." But since what is altered by no means either comes to be or perishes: as one who has stood too long in the sun, if from fair he has become dark, is said to be altered in colour, yet he has not come to be or perished, nor has any growth or diminution happened to him, nor is there any change of place; for someone remaining in one and the same place can be changed by certain affections coming from outside; he can also grow and decrease without alteration of quality: which Aristotle himself states thus.
passages.notes: '8i' read as 'si'. 'commutatio' rendered 'alteration' (qualitative change).

passages.original: Necnon etiam in vase haberi aliquid dicitur,ut triticum in modio,et vinum in dolio;haec, scilicet, ita haberi dicuntur, ut in vase. Dicitur etiam quis habere uxorem,quæ,scilicet significatio nulli supradictae communis est, sed (ut ipsi Aristoteli videtur) longe diversa est haec significatio ab habendi prædicamento;non enim proprie habemus uxores,sed quod habere quis dicatur uxorem, hoc significat habitare cum eo uxorern,habere enim habitare dicimus,ut est Socratem habent, id est cum Socrate habitant atque eum colunt.Quare ipse quo- queAristoteles inquit esse aliquos fortasse praeter eos qui dicantur habendi modos, hortaturque nos ad ulterioremaliquaminquisitionem,ut nos quoque quae ramus per quos,praeter priores dictos modos, alios possit habere praedicari.
passages.english: Furthermore, something is said to be had in a vessel, as wheat in a measure and wine in a jar; these are said to be had in this way, namely as in a vessel. Someone is also said to have a wife, and this meaning is common to none of those mentioned above. But (as it seems to Aristotle himself) this meaning is far different from the category of having. For we do not properly have wives; rather, that someone is said to have a wife means that the wife lives with him. For we use "have" for "dwell", as in "they have Socrates", that is, they dwell with Socrates and attend to him. Therefore Aristotle himself also says that there are perhaps some modes of having besides those that are mentioned, and he urges us to further inquiry, so that we too may seek through which [modes], besides the modes mentioned earlier, "to have" can be predicated in other ways.
passages.notes: The gloss of "habere" as "habitare" ("dwell") is the commentator's own etymological play. The last clause is awkward in the Latin ("per quos ... alios possit habere praedicari"), and the rendering is approximate.
